rebuttal.value:
Thank you to all the reviewers for their valuable feedback and comments. 

There are two common concerns raised by the reviewers: 1) the disambiguation between the current submission and Ref. 21 and 2) how the proposed framework differs from other existing efforts to assess data quality and ethicality. We respond to these concerns in the individual reviews below but also summarize our plan to address these concerns in this global rebuttal. 

Our current submission presents an evaluation framework for ML dataset documentation based on data curation principles developed iteratively **with** evidence supporting its feasible application for ML. In comparison, Ref. 21 presented the process around the initial construction of this framework and provided insights on the inner collaboration and challenges faced by an interdisciplinary team in this process. 

In Ref. 21, we did not present sufficient evidence to claim its feasibility. With further additions and refinements to the rubric and toolkit included in this current paper, we now present an updated evaluation framework. This new framework explains the qualities required by a well-curated dataset (thereby answering RQ 1). 

Further to this, we performed additional evaluations and those results are presented in this paper. There are **two** facets to evaluation: evaluating our framework and using our framework to evaluate data curation in ML. To provide robust norms, it has to be feasible to apply our framework consistently. This is why we iteratively refine the rubric and measure inter-rater reliability. Thus the additional results from round 4 help establish and solidify the feasibility of our framework (RQ 2). This then enables us to apply the framework to evaluate the state of data curation in ML in round 5 (RQ 3). 

We will also add some more text to the ‘Related Works’ section to succinctly differentiate our framework from other similar works. Particularly, similar evaluation or documentation frameworks often take the form of context documents and are used to provide documentation for datasets by detailing aspects of provenance and data collection and are particularly geared to answering ethical questions about the data [1–3]. One branch of these studies discusses the adoption of principles from archival studies and digital curation into dataset development processes for machine learning research [4–6]. The **distinctive** aspect of our framework is twofold, we firstly present a framework based on data curation principles and secondly, we do so by *operationalizing* these concepts. This advances prior literature by putting into practice concepts that were previously discussed in theory. 

We plan to clarify these points in the revisions, elaborate on the changes from the previous version of the rubric and toolkit, articulate the contributions more clearly, and address minor comments regarding figures, grammar, typos, etc. 

[1]	Emily M. Bender and Batya Friedman. 2018. Data Statements for Natural Language Processing: Toward Mitigating System Bias and Enabling Better Science. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics 6, (2018), 587–604. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00041

[2]	Kasia S Chmielinski, Sarah Newman, Matt Taylor, Josh Joseph, Kemi Thomas, Jessica Yurkofsky, and Yue Chelsea Qiu. The Dataset Nutrition Label (2nd Gen): Leveraging Context to Mitigate Harms in Artiﬁcial Intelligence.

[3]	Timnit Gebru, Jamie Morgenstern, Briana Vecchione, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan, Hanna Wallach, Hal Daumé III, and Kate Crawford. 2021. Datasheets for datasets. Commun. ACM 64, 12 (2021), 86–92. https://doi.org/10.1145/3458723

[4]	Eun Seo Jo and Timnit Gebru. 2020. Lessons from archives: strategies for collecting sociocultural data in machine learning. In Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, January 27, 2020. ACM, Barcelona Spain, 306–316. https://doi.org/10.1145/3351095.3372829

[5]	Susan Leavy, Eugenia Siapera, and Barry O’Sullivan. 2021. Ethical Data Curation for AI: An Approach based on Feminist Epistemology and Critical Theories of Race. In Proc. of  2021 AAAI/ACM Conf. on AI, Ethics, and Society, July 21, 2021. ACM, Virtual Event USA, 695–703. Retrieved November 11, 2022 from https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3461702.3462598

[6]	Nanna Bonde Thylstrup. 2022. The ethics and politics of data sets in the age of machine learning: deleting traces and encountering remains. Media, Culture & Society 44, 4 (May 2022), 655–671. https://doi.org/10.1177/01634437211060226

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your constructive feedback and insightful review. We agree with all of the points you raised and will make revisions to address each of them. In this response, we want to focus on key concerns and clarify the differentiation between our previous paper, Ref. 21, and this paper. 

In our previous paper, we discussed the *initial construction and design* of our evaluation framework consisting of the rubric and toolkit. Our paper accordingly presented the reflections from the process of designing the framework such as the benefits resulting from the diverse perspectives of an interdisciplinary team, the lessons learned while applying the framework, and how we used the data from the initial application of the rubric to iteratively refine it and yield more consistent evaluations. Ref. 21 was thus focused on reporting our reflections of the interdisciplinarity process applied in our venture to translate and operationalize data curation concepts, in practice, within ML. 

Our current paper briefly summarizes the work from Ref. 21 in the Methods section, lines 136-139. In Ref. 21, we presented results from a training round and rounds 1-3. After round 3, we updated and refined the criteria for 13 elements and added additional guidance in the toolkit for interpreting authenticity, reliability, and representativeness. The changes after round 3 are *only* provided in the current Appendix and are not present in Ref. 21. To claim that our framework is consistent, reliable, and accordingly feasible, an additional round of evaluations was performed (round 4 and disagreement review) which was presented in the current paper along with previous results. Previously we had introduced the framework but did not have solid evidence to make such claims. Therefore, it is only in our current paper that we have addressed RQ 1 with our most updated version of the framework and RQ 2 with the final fourth round of evaluations that firmly establishes the framework’s reliability through iteratively improving IRR results. We will accordingly clarify these points of differentiation, add references where needed, and more clearly articulate the contributions including that 35 new evaluation results are presented in this paper from the total 60. The results presented for R1 will also be shortened in order to reinforce the focus on R2-6. With the additional space allowed after reviews, we will also be able to add further discussion in Sections 4 and 5. 

Thank you for pointing out the difficulty in making comparisons between bars for Figures 2b and 2d, we will be changing these to grouped bars rather than stacked. We will also amend the caption for Figure 3. For Figure 1, we plan to label the number of datasets in each round to make the boxplot comparisons more useful.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your thoughtful feedback and review. Please see our responses below to address the opportunities for improvement.

*Subjectivity of the evaluation process* 
- In Ref. 21, we elaborately discussed the challenges and benefits of the subjectivity of the review process. Specifically we found that reviewers’ differing expertise meant that reviewers evaluated elements at different depths of analysis. On the other hand, the subjectivity of the rubric’s open-ended criteria presented greater opportunities for reviewers to engage in discussion and collaboration around how datasets can be curated. In our current paper, we provide the elements for which inconsistencies or disagreements were present in rounds 1-5 in Figure 7a and 7b in the Appendix. 

*Rationale for rubric elements*
- Ref. 21 details the process by which rubric elements were chosen. However, as pointed out by other reviewers, we will detail in the revisions the rationale behind the *changes* made to rubric evaluation criteria. 

*Fallibility of dataset documentation*
- Thank you for this insightful comment. As you correctly pointed out, using documentation to understand the curation process is not a substitute for being directly involved in the process or communicating with the dataset creators. As such, it is possible and ultimately a limitation that the reality of data curation is more complex than what is covered in documentation or our framework. In such cases, things can become overly simplified in the documentation and auditing process, e.g., box ticking instead of genuine reflection and evaluation. An ethnographic study of data curation from inside would yield different, additional, insights that we cannot provide. This is a limitation and future work that we will discuss in the revisions. 

*Limitations of standardizing framework*
- We agree that standardization can have downsides but based on the open-ended criteria of the framework and its expectation for descriptive evaluation, we hope that the rubric can enable generative discussion and collaboration rather than becoming a prescribed way to evaluate datasets’ documentation. Given that our framework is more reflective, flexible, comprehensive, and iterative (rather than being a benchmarking tool), we believe we have reduced the limitations introduced by standardizing. 

*Number of datasets evaluated*
- Using the rubric to evaluate a dataset can take up to 60 minutes. In order to perform triple coding for the training round and rounds 1-4 and double coding for round 5, we were limited to the evaluation of 60 randomly chosen datasets. This number of 60 datasets represents 150 hours of evaluation effort and approximately 10 hours of effort in disagreement reviews totalling 160 hours altogether. 

*Dataset creators’ involvement*
- Currently, external dataset creators to the team were not consulted in the creation of the framework (though team members have experience producing and evaluating datasets of comparable size and complexity). However this is an opportunity for future work. Feedback from dataset creators can shed more light on how to improve the evaluation criteria, whether there are elements which can be added to the rubric, and how the toolkit can be improved to provide any needed resources. 

*Composition of reviewers* 
- The composition of the reviewers and their expertise is outlined in the Appendix of Ref. 21. The selection of the reviewers is outlined in the current Appendix. We also discuss how exactly the diversity of the group helped in the construction of the rubric in the current Appendix (in Section D.4). We do not expect ML dataset creators to require any prior training or expertise in data curation to be able to use this evaluation framework. However, we recommend using the toolkit to become familiarized with data curation, its concepts and literature, and be able to better apply the evaluation framework. 

*Intended usage of evaluation framework results and usage of framework to change dataset creators’ practice* 
- We intend for the evaluation framework to be used by two types of users. The first is dataset creators who can use the rubric as a resource to prompt and facilitate critical engagement and reflection throughout their dataset creation process. The second group is dataset re-users who can use the framework to evaluate datasets prior to reuse by applying the rubric to determine gaps that require further documentation and areas where bias can be introduced. In both cases, we aim for the rubric to be a practical and useful resource for researchers to engage with the dataset creation process using a data curation lens. This also means that we *do not* intend for the rubric to be used to rank datasets and this is also the reason why quantitative criteria were not used (and rather ‘Full’, ‘Partial’, ‘None’). Instead, by using the framework, dataset creators can know which areas need better documentation to enable more transparency and accountability of their data design decisions. On the other hand, dataset re-users can better know whether the dataset is appropriate for their task.


The details outlined above will be more clearly articulated in the revised paper.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your feedback and comments. We appreciate your recognition of the efforts around the construction of the framework. Please see our responses below addressing the opportunities for improvement and limitations. 

We plan to more clearly disambiguate between the contributions of our previous paper introducing the evaluation framework, Ref. 21, and this current submission as mentioned by other reviewers as well. In Ref. 21, we outlined the rationale behind the guidelines. However, in this submission, we provided an *updated* toolkit and rubric. As such, we plan to more clearly articulate the rationale behind the *changes* as compared to Ref. 21. For example, we removed one rubric element, ‘integrity’, and consolidated its criteria within ‘authenticity’. We refined the criteria for several guidelines including adding details relevant for evaluating synthetic data. The exact details regarding these changes will be included in the revised paper within ‘Section 3: Methods under Evaluation Framework’. 

Additionally, as raised by Reviewer MJgK as well, there are already existing efforts to assess data quality such as checklists, datasheets and so on. Our framework, used to assess the state of data curation in the NeurIPS D&B track, is rooted in data curation principles and concepts. By drawing from data curation literature, we are able to identify strengths and weaknesses in current curation practices and recommend targeted improvements by incorporating data curation methods where they are most needed. We plan to more clearly differentiate between our proposed set of guidelines and other frameworks such as datasheets, nutrition labels, data statements, and so on. By providing a framework in the form of a rubric, we move away from the prescriptive nature of checklists which can impede critical reflection and *instead* increase the ability for evaluators to engage in discussion, debate, and reflect on diverse perspectives and approaches to data practices. This approach to the examination of data practices is in line with current literature about domain-specific data practices and the need for contextually-aware curation practices.  

Lastly, as correctly raised, each data re-user or researcher will have specific applications for their datasets and will want documentation regarding the same. For example, the recommended test/train split being documented while of importance to ML data users, our current framework is based on data curation principles and thus did not consider this criteria. However, at present this is out of scope. Our framework includes criteria required by *all* data users but not the special interests. Recommendations to improve the rubric such as these can become part of evolving documentation such as the toolkit. This also points to open questions, to consider in the future, about how the toolkit can help in addressing personalized criteria. 

For the final paper, we will address all remaining concerns including typos and other minor grammatical errors.

Thank you for your feedback and positive comments. We will definitely look towards creating a simple website to facilitate easy use of the toolkit and rubric.

We plan to revise the paper to add more clarity in how our proposed framework can be differentiated from other frameworks that evaluate ethical and fair uses of data. ML studies on data practices (“…what and how data are collected, managed, used, interpreted, reused, deposited, curated, and so on…” [2:55]) also called dataset development and data work most closely resemble examinations of the processes of data curation (despite often using the term to connote data collection, e.g., [5–7]). Other works in this space discuss the importance of documentation and propose new frameworks for it [1, 3, 4], review intrinsic and extrinsic biases in the dataset development process [9–11], and highlight the power dynamics involved in data quality, data work, and documentation [8]. In contrast, our framework enables the application of data curation principles and concepts in practice. 

We also plan to more clearly articulate that this paper provides an updated version of the toolkit and rubric as compared to Ref. 21, as suggested by other reviewers as well. 

[1]	Emily M. Bender and Batya Friedman. 2018. Data Statements for Natural Language Processing: Toward Mitigating System Bias and Enabling Better Science. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics 6, (2018), 587–604. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00041

[2]	Christine L. Borgman. 2017. Big Data, Little Data, No Data: Scholarship in the Networked World. MIT Press.

[3]	Kasia S Chmielinski, Sarah Newman, Matt Taylor, Josh Joseph, Kemi Thomas, Jessica Yurkofsky, and Yue Chelsea Qiu. The Dataset Nutrition Label (2nd Gen): Leveraging Context to Mitigate Harms in Artiﬁcial Intelligence.

[5]	Kenneth Holstein, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan, Hal Daumé, Miro Dudik, and Hanna Wallach. 2019. Improving Fairness in Machine Learning Systems: What Do Industry Practitioners Need? In Proc. CHI’2019, May 02, 2019. ACM, Glasgow Scotland Uk, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1145/3290605.3300830

title.value: Important work; clarification needed on overlap with previous publication

summary_and_contributions.value: In this paper, the authors apply their dataset documentation evaluation framework to 30 datasets from the last few years of NeurIPS D&B and summarize the findings, yielding interesting insights into the state of dataset documentation practices in this track. Based on these findings, they go on to suggest strategies and resources for improving dataset documentation at NeurIPS D&B.

review.value:
The dataset documentation framework demonstrated in this paper is important, high-quality work that is of clear significance to the ML community. The provided rubric and toolkit are nicely organized and prepared, and I foresee them being useful in the data curation process.

However, I have some concerns about how the extent of the contributions of this paper compared to Ref. 21 (the authors’ previous publication from FAccT 2024) are portrayed. Upon an initial reading of the paper, it had been my understanding that the evaluation framework, including the rubric and toolkit, were considered contributions of this paper and not of the previous publication. Based on some of the text and the inclusion of the rubric and toolkit in the Appendix of this paper, I think this was a reasonable conclusion. I understand now that the rubric is not one of the primary contributions of this paper; rather this paper’s contribution is the application of the rubric to the NeurIPS D&B datasets (the 30 datasets of Round 5 + the 5 datasets for disagreement review in Round 4). While I do see the merits in this being a separate publication, I do not believe this to be conveyed clearly enough in the text, which I detail later in the review.

strengths.value:
- The rubric and toolkit are resources that have the potential to be useful throughout the data curation process, and the authors have done substantial work in making these tools usable and ensuring they are reliable.
- The application of the rubric to datasets at NeurIPS D&B provided useful insights into current practices and identified major opportunities for improvement, which can now be grounded in quantitative evidence as a result of this study.
- Beyond just identifying areas of improvement, the authors also make concrete suggestions for how to go about making these improvements in Section 5.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
The biggest opportunity for improvement is to clearly differentiate between the contributions of this paper compared to Ref. 21. 

Concretely, my areas of concern in this regard include:

- Section 1, Contributions (lines 50-52): “[W]e present a systematic dataset documentation evaluation framework to organize the assessment of curation practices for ML dataset development.”

Including this sentence in the Contributions section without a reference to Ref. 21 is misleading.

- Section 1, Contributions (lines 52-55): “The framework is composed of a rubric and toolkit developed through an iterative multi-stage process to arrive at the rubric elements relevant for evaluation and corresponding criteria for their assessment, as well as supplementary material packaged as a toolkit to aid in the application of the rubric.”

Again, putting this in the Contributions section leads one to believe this is a contribution of this paper and not of Ref. 21. However, the rubric and toolkit are already published as the Appendix to Ref. 21. If changes were made to the rubric and toolkit between that publication and this one, perhaps as a result of the disagreement review in Round 4, then it should be clearly stated that this is an updated rubric. Otherwise, Ref. 21 should be cited as the source of the rubric rather than including it here.

- Section 1, Contributions (lines 55-56): “Here, we establish the feasibility of this framework as an auditing tool for dataset documentation by performing a systematic evaluation of a sample set of 60 datasets”

If I have understood correctly, the first 25/60 datasets were analyzed in the previous publication, 5 additional datasets in Round 4, and then the 30 datasets that are the basis for the primary analyses in this paper.

- Section 3, Research Questions (lines 127-129): “[W]e examine (1) What constitutes a well curated dataset? (2) How feasible is the adoption of data curation principles to assess ML datasets? and (3) What is the state of data curation at NeurIPS and how can it be further advanced?”

Two of the three questions posed here seem to be addressed by the work of Ref. 21 rather than this work. Only RQ3 is of primary focus to this work (though it is certainly based on the answers to 1 and 2).

- Section 3, Evaluation Framework, Iterations, Consistency: These subsections describe the processes that preceded the final application to the 30 final datasets. My understanding is that most of this work was already reported in Ref. 21. It is not clear to me why it should be lengthily summarized again in this publication. I can understand that this is a new tool and that its reliability needs to be established before it can be meaningfully applied. However, I think this could be done much more succinctly and with increased reference to Ref. 21, to make explicit that this publication is not meant to report on these stages of the work.

- Section 4, R1: “Inter-rater reliability suggests the evaluations are consistent and reliable.”

Similarly here, it is my understanding that the reliability of the framework was established in Ref. 21 (e.g., Figure 2b in Ref. 21 has a strong overlap with Figure 1a in this paper) and that this work should primarily focus on the results of Round 5, i.e., R2-R6.
Appendix: There is a substantial overlap between the Appendix of this paper and that of Ref. 21, including the rubric and toolkit. The rubric and toolkit should be removed from the Appendix, and they should instead be referenced where they are already published in Ref. 21.

Secondary opportunities for improvement:

- Figure 1b + 1d: The use of a stacked bar chart here makes it quite challenging to compare the proportions. Green bars can be compared since they line up at the bottom; red bars can be compared since they line up at the top, but it is almost impossible to compare orange bars. The bulk of the findings seem as though they could be rooted in Figures 1a and 1c, which are far easier to interpret, and Figures 1b + 1d could be removed or reworked for the Appendix.

- Figure 1a: There are differing numbers of datasets in Training (10 datasets), Rounds 1-4 (5 datasets each), and Round 5 (30 datasets). Are the bars on the boxplot meaningful to compare?

- Figure 3 caption: “In both cases there is no significant change across time”

I suggest avoiding the loaded word “significant” in the absence of a statistical analysis.

limitations.value: Yes, Section 5.3 provides a well-rounded summary of the limitations, and I am hard-pressed to think of potential negative societal impacts of this work.

correctness.value: To my knowledge, all claims made in the paper are correct (excluding any issues discussed above).

clarity.value: Yes, the paper is well written with minimal spelling and grammatical errors.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper does a good job of connecting their evaluation and findings to previous research on data practices in ML and data curation. As discussed in detail above, I do not feel the distinction between the contributions of this paper and the contributions of Ref. 21 were made sufficiently clear, however.

documentation.value: Yes, the dataset is maintained in Zenodo and is well-documented and licensed.

ethics.value: I do not think the submission requires further ethical discussion or review.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: I encourage the authors to consider reworking the text to remove redundancies with Ref. 21 to the extent possible and to make this submission more distinct. Not only will this disambiguate the two papers’ contributions, but it will also leave more space within the tight page constraints for the authors to engage with the primary goals of this submission, e.g., discuss their findings more deeply in Section 4 or their suggestions more thoroughly in Section 5.

You are encouraged to think through whether any critical points are missing and provide these as feedback for the authors.

correctness.description: Are the claims made in the submission correct? If the submission is a dataset, it is constructed in a sound way? If it is a benchmark, are the evaluation methods and experiment design appropriate and performed correctly?

relation_to_prior_work.description: Is it clearly discussed how this work differs from previous contributions?

documentation.description: For datasets, is there sufficient detail on data collection and organization, availability and maintenance, and ethical and responsible use? title.value: A valuable assessment of the quality of data documentation during the first three years of D&B at NeurIPS

summary_and_contributions.value:
This submission looks at patterns within the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track from 2021 - 2023. The team have developed a systematic dataset documentation evaluation framework to organise the assessment of curation practices for ML dataset development. 

In their own words, the team's research questions are "What are the strengths and weaknesses of NeurIPS dataset documentation practices considered through a data curation lens? In other words, how well curated are NeurIPS datasets and benchmarks? To study this, we examine (1) What constitutes a well curated dataset? (2) How feasible is the adoption of data curation principles to assess ML datasets? and (3) What is the state of data curation at NeurIPS and how can it be further advanced?"

The framework was applied to manually assess 60 ML datasets in three steps: 1) 25 datasets in 4 rounds of assessment and iterative development, 2) inter-rater reliability assessed on 5 new datasets, 3) evaluation of 30 additional datasets to "evaluate current practices of data curation in ML dataset development and areas in which improvement was needed". The rubric ended up with 18 elements across 5 categories: scope, ethicality and reflexivity, data pipeline, data quality, and data management. There was high inter rater reliability.

The team found that documentation quality varies widely across datasets with even the best performing paper only scoring "full" on 50% of standards of excellence. They also found that NeurIPS guidelines prioritise model-work adjacent documentation, with NeurIPS papers performing well on the context, purpose, motivation, suitability and reliability elements 100% fulfilled. They found that documentation was rarely context aware and often remains incomplete. And that there have been no improvements over the last 3 years.

The paper includes a discussion of how to improve data curation at NeurIPS with strategies and resources that are curated particularly well and a proposal for peer review.

review.value:
I thought this was an excellent paper. I really enjoyed reading it and I found it very applicable to this track. I'm particularly impressed that the NeurIPS D&B track are so motivated to self reflect and continue to improve.

I thought the background section was short, to the point, and very clear. I appreciated the iterative development and assessment of the rubric. I think the recommendations are strong and I hope that this work continues to integrate with existing work assessing the responsible curation and management of data throughout its lifecycle.

There is a lot of information in the appendix and in my review I've spent a while wondering if that's a strength or an area to improve - is there a way to point the reader to those resources more easily. I've ultimately decided that the authors have balanced the content of the paper well and I can't see ways to improve it. There's just a lot of work to show off!

strengths.value:
I thought this paper was really well written with a clear purpose and target audience. I appreciated that the authors conducted an inter rater reliability assessment.

Given the team's findings that there hasn't been any improvements in the data documentation over time it is particularly important that these findings are shared with the NeurIPS D&B community.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: I was missing in this paper how the work is distinct from existing efforts to assess data quality. I understand that the work has already been published in reference 21 but it may help the reader to add a little more information about why a new toolkit is necessary!

limitations.value:
The authors have addressed 4 limitations: bias introduced by a random sample, bias introduced based on descriptive and interpretive evaluations, bias introduced from within reviewer discrepancies when assessing different data sets, and the lack of integrating domain specific information about the datasets to provide more curated insights.

I think these limitations are small and well justified.

correctness.value: Yes. All the claims made in the submission are well justified.

clarity.value: Yes. I thought it was an excellent read. Very clear and insightful.

relation_to_prior_work.value:
I wasn't very clear on how this framework compared to others that exist for assessing the responsible / ethical / FAIR or fair uses of data.

But given the specific focus on assessing NeurIPS D&B submissions over the first 3 years I think the team can justify curating a more bespoke rubric and toolkit.

documentation.value: Yes - the data and code are available for interrogation. The toolkit is excellent and provides extensive support for anyone wanting to apply the assessment to their own work.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: Thank you for writing all this up! Please make a (simple) website and make it really easy for others to use your hard work :) I look forward to citing the paper.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces a set of guidelines that can be used to evaluate the thoroughness of a dataset's documentation. The authors establish their guidelines through an iterative refinement process of several rounds so that they can ensure that the guidelines can be applied fairly and objectively. The paper applies the guidelines to 60 recent NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks track papers, finding that there are major potential gaps in documentation for certain guideline categories like environmental footprint. The Appendix of this paper is very valuable, as it contains the guidelines and several example applications of them to real datasets/papers.

review.value: Overall, I found this paper well written and clear. I would have liked to see the guidelines in the main paper but they are nevertheless clearly articulated in the Appendix. Personally, I do not find the paper to be too novel or exciting (there have been papers on checklists before in recent years), but this is a subjective view. For me, I initially disagreed with the "environmental footprint" guideline, but the paper's discussion on this guideline provoked me to reflect on it, which encapsulates the value of the paper. See strengths and weaknesses in ("Opportunities for Improvement") below.

strengths.value:
- Very detailed appendix with the full list of guidelines and several examples of them being applied to real papers.
- The guidelines are not constructed arbitrarily, but are refined through an iterative application process in order to help ensure correctness/objectivity.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: - I would have liked more discussion on the rationale behind some of the guidelines. However, many of the guidelines in the proposed list are accepted by the broader community as being important (e.g., it is widely accepted that "data annotation" needs to be discussed in papers that release new datasets).

limitations.value: Limitations are discussed in Section 5.3. One potential limitation is that the guidelines do not cover "my set of important guidelines". For instance, as a researcher, I am particularly interested in whether a dataset is split into train/test splits adequately to minimize leakage across test-train splits. Other researchers will have other various guidelines that are important to them but may not be fully represented in the proposed guidelines.

correctness.value: The authors made a large effort in ensuring that their proposed guidelines are applicable and can be applied consistently. They did this through an iterative refinement process with several human annotators.

clarity.value: Overall, the paper is clearly written.

relation_to_prior_work.value: There have been many other "checklists" proposed in the past few years. A discussion of any overlap between this proposed set of guidelines and these other checklists would be welcome.

documentation.value: The Appendix provides ample documentation and supplementary material.

ethics.value: I do not suspect any ethical concerns with this submission.

title.value: Well considered and tested framework for evaluation

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper illustrates a comprehensive benchmarking tool for dataset creation practices and communication, which is of great interest to the D&B track. The authors underscore the importance of dataset curation practices, and assessing previous datasets and papers within the D&B track. They then propose a framework for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of datasets. This assessment highlights specific areas for improvement within the field such as consistency of documentation, environmental impact, broader ethical considerations and data management.

review.value: This paper provides a relevant and timely intervention into the field of dataset development. The framework presented is detailed and the methodology clearly discussed.

strengths.value:
The clear strength of this paper is the framework developed by the authors. It is clear that this framework has been well-considered and tested. The iterative methods through which it was constructed are detailed well within the paper. Moreover, the supplementary materials do a good job of answering particular questions that I had about the methodology while reading the paper. 

This framework may be particularly useful for dataset creators to consider within their practices, users of datasets to consider which dataset may be most appropriate for their task, and auditors of datasets as a framework for understanding and evaluating datasets from publicly available information. The disagreement review highlights the need to think about the challenges of assessing datasets and the benefits of collaboration. 

The findings also clearly identify a niche to be addressed with dataset documentation, that varies widely across papers. The findings highlight that dataset documentation is often incomplete and does not consider the broader context of the dataset, such as environmental impact. I was particularly struck that there had been little to no improvement in documentation practices over time.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
Some additional areas to consider are below:

- I found the inter rater reliability variability quite interesting, from 0.45 to 0.94. There might be opportunity here to reflect to the subjectivity of the review process. While I do not think that such a qualitative evaluation of datasets is inherently limited, this does point towards the value of collaboratively assessing datasets. While the paper does address the median IRR (0.90), the variability of IRR could be addressed in the paper. I would also love more information on what were some of the more disagreed upon or discussed factors by reviewers were?

- The evaluation framework is clearly extensive. While many of the elements are well cited in the supplementary materials, some could be improved. This would go a long way to answer the question why certain elements are on the framework. I was also wondering if there were certain elements that were specifically left off the framework - i.e., elements that were discussed by the team but were ultimately not included. 

- This framework is particularly focused on how datasets can be evaluated from the documentation provided, allowing for audits to take place without access to the dataset creation team. However, it made me wonder about the fallibility of dataset documentation that may simplify complex processes (sometimes due to conference deadlines or page limits). This might be an additional limitation of the study to consider. 

- Are there potential limitations of a framework becoming standardized? For example, we have seen with other benchmarks how certain frameworks for evaluation have created an intense focus on improving performance in certain areas at the neglect of others.

limitations.value: The paper addresses some of the potential limitations of their work.

correctness.value: The claims made are clear, and though this is not a dataset, the evaluation framework is largely well explained.

relation_to_prior_work.value: This paper clearly connects to prior work on this topic, and provides a good 'further reading' section in the Appendix.

documentation.value: The paper provides a clear framework to evaluate datasets, as well as substantial supplementary material that details how this framework was constructed as well as addressing many additional questions that I had.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
Some additional questions that I had: 

- Why were only 60 datasets analysed? How was this number reached? 

- I couldn't see anywhere whether dataset creators or users were consulted in creating this framework? How might it be honed with additional involvement? 

- Who were the reviewers? How were they selected? What were their backgrounds and forms of expertise? Are they dataset creators or users? While the paper mentions the "diverse perspectives" of reviewers, additional clarification here would be beneficial. This might also be useful for insight into whether 'anyone' can use this framework or whether it requires some form of expertise. 

- Is this framework intended to be used to rank datasets, or to suggest the most appropriate dataset for a task? How might this work? How might the nature of these assessments hinder/challenge a comparative approach to dataset ranking and evaluation? 

- While this framework is mainly used to guide the evaluation of datasets, how might dataset creators use it to improve their practice? Are there any additional considerations for that population?

title.value: The State of Data Curation at NeurIPS: An Assessment of Dataset Development Practices in the Datasets and Benchmarks Track

abstract.value: Data curation is a field with origins in librarianship and archives, whose scholarship and thinking on data issues go back centuries, if not millennia. The field of machine learning is increasingly observing the importance of data curation to the advancement of both applications and fundamental understanding of machine learning models -- evidenced not least by the creation of the Datasets and Benchmarks track itself. This work provides an analysis of recent dataset development practices at NeurIPS through the lens of data curation. We present an evaluation framework for dataset documentation, consisting of a rubric and toolkit developed through a thorough literature review of data curation principles. We use the framework to systematically assess the strengths and weaknesses in current dataset development practices of 60 datasets published in the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track from 2021-2023. We summarize key findings and trends. Results indicate greater need for documentation about environmental footprint, ethical considerations, and data management. We suggest targeted strategies and resources to improve documentation in these areas and  provide recommendations for the NeurIPS peer-review process that prioritize rigorous data curation in ML. We also provide guidelines for dataset developers on the use of our rubric as a standalone tool. Finally, we provide results in the format of a dataset that showcases aspects of recommended data curation practices. Our rubric and results are of interest for improving data curation practices broadly in the field of ML as well as to data curation and science and technology studies scholars studying practices in ML. Our aim is to support continued improvement in interdisciplinary research on dataset practices, ultimately improving the reusability and reproducibility of new datasets and benchmarks, enabling standardized and informed human oversight, and strengthening the foundation of rigorous and responsible ML research.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
